awd_titl_txt: SBIR Phase I: AI-Driven Platform for Prior Authorization Automation and Workflow Optimization in Oncology Specialty Healthcare
awd_abstract_narration:
The broader impact/commercial potential of this Small Business Innovation Research (SBIR) Phase I project lies in transforming oncology prior authorization (PA) processes through artificial intelligence (AI) automation. Current PA systems are labor-intensive, causing costly delays in life-saving cancer treatments. This innovation aims to streamline treatment approvals, reducing administrative burdens and supporting faster patient access to care. By leveraging natural language processing and machine learning, the platform could improve workflow efficiency, decrease PA processing times,  and increase initial PA approval rates. The commercial potential is significant, with the U.S. oncology clinics market of $454 million. The business model follows a subscription-based software approach, ensuring scalability and recurring revenue. The company projects over $8 million in revenue and break even by year three, positioning itself for long-term growth and acquisition by major healthcare IT firms. This project will advance scientific understanding of AI applications in healthcare administration while providing a scalable, competitive solution to a critical inefficiency in US healthcare.

This Small Business Innovation Research (SBIR) Phase I project aims to develop and validate an AI-driven platform to automate prior authorization (PA) processing in oncology clinics, addressing a critical bottleneck in timely cancer treatment. Current PA workflows are manual, time-consuming, and prone to missing documents and errors, delaying treatment initiation by an average of two weeks and leading to increased patient mortality. This project will integrate natural language processing (NLP), machine learning (ML), and reinforcement learning (RL) to streamline PA submission, predict approval likelihoods, and optimize workflows. The research objectives include (1) developing NLP models to extract key clinical data from unstructured medical records, (2) training ML models to predict PA outcomes with high accuracy based on historical and real-time data, and (3) implementing RL-driven workflow automation to optimize PA submissions and follow-ups. The outcomes will establish a foundation for broader deployment across multiple specialties, enhancing healthcare operational efficiency nationwide.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

por.por_cntn:
Insurance prior authorization is the process health plans use to determine whether certain treatments, medications, or medical services will be covered. In cancer care, this process can be complex, time-sensitive, and consequential for patients. Clinic staff may need to gather information from multiple medical records, interpret changing payer requirements, respond to requests for additional information, and manage denials, appeals, or physician reviews. These administrative steps can consume substantial staff time, create uncertainty for patients and families, and delay treatment readiness.

With support from NSF SBIR Phase I Award 2507367, Hidalga Technologies investigated whether artificial intelligence and workflow technology could help community oncology practices manage prior authorization more efficiently while preserving provider oversight. The research was conducted in collaboration with an Arkansas community oncology practice, which contributed de-identified oncology data, operational workflow knowledge, and review of study findings.

The project advanced hidalga™ from an early concept to a functioning, human-governed prior authorization platform designed to assemble clinical evidence, identify higher-risk cases, guide staff review, and maintain a traceable record of evidence and decisions. Phase I combined two years of de-identified community oncology data with natural language processing, machine learning, workflow analysis, software engineering, and customer discovery. The research included more than 148,000 administrative workflow free-text records from over 24,000 patients and approximately 96,000 resolved prior authorization cases.

The project demonstrated strong technical feasibility. Combining structured medical-record information with clinical notes achieved an average F1 score of 0.97 across evaluated data fields, indicating that information dispersed across different parts of the medical record can be rapidly assembled with high reliability. A denial-risk model achieved a ROC-AUC of 0.88, demonstrating strong ability to distinguish higher-risk from lower-risk cases. Together, these capabilities could help oncology teams identify missing information earlier and focus review on cases most likely to need additional attention, reducing repeated paperwork, appeals, and avoidable treatment delays.

The research also clarified where delays occur. Median time from a clinic visit to creation of a prior authorization case was approximately 0.5 days, compared with 64 days from case creation to the recorded payer decision. Strict-policy payer groups had a median turnaround time of approximately 65 days, compared with 35 days for lenient-policy groups. These findings suggest that improving clinic speed alone may not solve the problem. Better payer-specific evidence preparation and follow-up may also be necessary to reduce delays.

Workflow modeling further suggested that improved case preparation and next-action selection could reduce turnaround time under simulated conditions. These estimates establish concrete hypotheses for live pilot testing. Trial-associated cases also showed substantially more rework, resubmissions, appeals, and peer-to-peer reviews than standard-of-care cases, demonstrating that administrative burden extends beyond simple turnaround time, particularly for patients receiving complex or investigational therapies.

The broader societal value of this work is the potential to make access to cancer treatment more predictable. If validated prospectively, hidalga™ could help reduce preventable administrative delays, decrease repeated documentation and appeals, improve continuity of care, and reduce the uncertainty patients and families experience while waiting for insurance decisions. It could also allow oncology staff to spend less time searching records and managing repetitive administrative work and more time supporting patients.

Phase I also represents an Arkansas-based health technology innovation effort. Hidalga Technologies developed the research, secure healthcare-data infrastructure, interoperability architecture, machine-learning systems, and workflow technology in collaboration with an Arkansas oncology provider and other regional partners. The project also received a $50,000 SBIR matching award from the Arkansas Economic Development Commission, extending the federal investment in Arkansas-based research and technology commercialization. This work contributes to regional technical capacity in healthcare AI, clinical interoperability, cybersecurity, and data science while addressing a problem experienced by community cancer practices nationally.

NSF funding ultimately established the scientific, technical, and governance foundation for controlled multi-clinic testing. The next phase will determine whether the improvements demonstrated retrospectively and in simulation translate into measurable reductions in administrative burden, treatment-readiness delays, and uncertainty for oncology practices, patients, and families.
